## Overview

The year 2026 constitutes a decisive inflection point in the post-Apollo lunar era, marked by the formal emergence of two rival, permanently-crewed lunar surface architectures: the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's (NASA) Artemis Base Camp and the China–Russia International Lunar Research Station (ILRS). These programs are not merely sequential extensions of robotic reconnaissance; they represent a fundamental strategic shift from flags-and-footprints exploration toward sustained off-world industrial capability, with in-situ resource utilization (ISRU)—particularly water ice mining in the lunar south polar region—serving as the linchpin of both designs. As of 2026, NASA has transitioned from concept formulation to active procurement and phased deployment, announcing the Moon Base initiative on March 24, 2026, during the agency's "Ignition" event at which it unveiled a series of transformative initiatives aligned with the U.S. National Space Policy [26], [5]. Concurrently, the China–Russia ILRS continues its parallel maturation through a sequence of robotic precursor missions and formal intergovernmental agreements, creating a de facto competitive framework for permanent off-planet settlement that is unprecedented in human history.
